newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle Atlantis is U.S. space woman's ticket home.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle Atlantis is U.S. space woman's ticket home.

text.p: Shannon Lucid, in her sixth month aboard the Russian Mir space station, on Sunday was depending on good weather and no equipment malfunctions for the shuttle Atlantis to finally get her home.
Atlantis, running six weeks late, is due to blast off from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre before dawn on Monday to collect Lucid from the remote orbiting outpost.
"We're Shannon's prime ticket home," said Paul Dye, the flight director who will orchestrate the mission from NASA's control centre in Houston. "We will be real happy to see her back."

Lucid has been working aboard Mir since March and is the first of six U.S. astronauts who will staff the Russian station into 1998. Her place on Mir will be taken by John Blaha, a former fighter pilot and veteran of four shuttle missions.
Atlantis is due home on Sept. 26, ending Lucid's 188-day mission, a record for a woman and the longest space flight by an American.

The shuttle was supposed to have picked up Lucid, a 53-year-old biochemist, and dropped off her replacement in early August, but rocket booster problems and menacing hurricanes have delayed her return.
Without Atlantis, Lucid is effectively stranded in space. NASA has no concrete plans for Lucid's return if the shuttle suffers another major delay or an accident of some kind.

"It's extremely unlikely, but if for some reason we were delayed for months on Atlantis, then we would just have to evaluate the situation and decide at what time and how she needed to come home," said Frank Culbertson, who heads NASA's shuttle-Mir effort.

A Soyuz capsule, which transports cosmonauts to and from the station, could be used in an emergency to get her home. However, this would be a last resort because her two Russian crewmates would have to accompany her, leaving the Mir station unmanned.
If the outpost were abandoned, it could quickly become uninhabitable because it needs constant maintenance to keep its complex systems operating.

"It would be a major impact to the overall programme if we brought her home in the Soyuz," said Culbertson. "And that's really the only other option at this point. There's not another Soyuz scheduled until February and Atlantis is the only shuttle that can do this."
Atlantis' mission, the 79th of the shuttle programme and fourth to dock with Mir, is due to get underway at 4:54 a.m. EDT (0854 GMT) on Monday.

After matching orbits with the sprawling Russian space complex, shuttle commander Bill Readdy will gently ease Atlantis towards the station's docking port and with a nudge from the shuttle's manoeuvring jets lock the two 100-ton spacecraft together.
Atlantis and Mir will remain docked for five days while Lucid and Blaha switch places and cargo is moved to and from the station.
Atlantis is carrying about 4,600 pounds (2,070 kgs) of supplies and equipment for Mir and will return to earth with 2,200 pounds (990 kgs) of scientific samples and other gear from the station.
Blaha will remain aboard the station until January when Atlantis will return to collect him and deliver his replacement, Jerry Linenger.
